history.ask: Last menstrual period (women of childbearing age)
Known kidney disease or falling urine output
Chest pain or sweating with the vomiting

red_flags: Feculent or persistent bilious vomiting with distension and absolute constipation
Signs of severe dehydration or shock — hypotension, tachycardia, confusion
Vomiting accompanied by chest pain and diaphoresis
New severe headache, neck stiffness, or effortless early-morning vomiting
Drowsiness with deep sighing (Kussmaul) breathing in a diabetic
exam: Vital signs including postural blood pressure — quantify dehydration
Assess hydration: mucous membranes, skin turgor, capillary refill
Inspect sclerae for icterus and conjunctivae for pallor
Inspect the abdomen for distension and visible peristalsis
Palpate for epigastric or right-upper-quadrant tenderness, guarding, masses
Auscultate bowel sounds — tinkling or absent suggests obstruction
Elicit a succussion splash if gastric outlet obstruction is suspected
Bedside neurological screen if headache or vertigo: nystagmus, gait, fundoscopy

investigations.why: Immediately rules diabetic ketoacidosis in or out in any vomiting diabetic or newly polyuric patient
Ketonuria supports DKA; heavy specific gravity confirms dehydration; a positive pregnancy test explains the vomiting and redirects the whole workup
Rules uremia in or out as the cause, and quantifies hypokalemia/alkalosis produced by the vomiting itself
Leukocytosis supports gastroenteritis or obstruction with ischemia; unexplained anemia raises a bleeding peptic ulcer
Raised transaminases with bilirubin rule in acute hepatitis behind RUQ ache, jaundice, or dark urine
Excludes pancreatitis mimicking simple gastritis when epigastric pain accompanies the vomiting
Inferior myocardial infarction can present as vomiting alone — mandatory when chest pain, diaphoresis, or risk factors are present
Air–fluid levels rule intestinal obstruction in when vomitus is bilious/feculent with distension
Second-line — if hematemesis, refractory epigastric symptoms, or unexplained vomiting > 2 weeks: confirms peptic ulcer/gastritis or gastric outlet obstruction

supports: Acute onset < 48 h with diarrhea and/or fever
Similar illness in household or a suspicious meal
No alarm findings on abdominal exam
Bilious or feculent vomitus with colicky pain and distension
Known diabetes or new thirst and polyuria
Drowsiness out of proportion to vomiting
Known kidney disease or falling urine output
Missed period in a woman of childbearing age
No fever and a normal abdomen
Vomiting with chest pain or diaphoresis
Minimal abdominal tenderness despite marked symptoms
